DLEC-CTX-G1.title: ECON 214 Week 6 slides - Price elasticity of demand
DLEC-CTX-G1.text:
ECON 214 - Intermediate Microeconomics
Week 6 Lecture Slides: Price Elasticity of Demand
Prof. Adaeze Okonkwo-Hale | Harlow State University | Section 002

Slide 1 - Learning goals
- Compute own-price elasticity of demand using the course's midpoint convention
- Classify demand as elastic, inelastic, or unit elastic
- Connect elasticity to what happens to total revenue when price changes

Slide 2 - Definition
Own-price elasticity of demand measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a change in the good's own price:
E = (% change in quantity demanded) / (% change in price)
Because demand slopes down, the raw ratio is negative.

Slide 3 - ECON 214 convention (read this carefully)
In this course we ALWAYS use the midpoint (arc) formula unless a question explicitly says "point elasticity":
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / ((Q1 + Q2) / 2)
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / ((P1 + P2) / 2)
We report own-price elasticity as an absolute value, rounded to two decimals. So you write 1.22, not -1.22.
Many textbooks (including the optional Marchetti text) divide by the starting values instead. That gives a different number for the same data, and it gives a different number depending on whether the price goes up or down. The midpoint version gives the same answer in both directions, which is why we use it.

Slide 4 - Classification (using the absolute value |E|)
- |E| > 1: elastic
- |E| < 1: inelastic
- |E| = 1 exactly: unit elastic
Note: 1.00 after rounding counts as unit elastic on problem sets and exams.

Slide 5 - Worked example: the Quad coffee cart
The coffee cart outside Benning Hall raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60. Daily sales fall from 500 cups to 400 cups.
Step 1: % change in Q = (400 - 500) / 450 = -0.2222, i.e. -22.2%
Step 2: % change in P = (3.60 - 3.00) / 3.30 = 0.1818, i.e. 18.2%
Step 3: E = -22.2% / 18.2% = -1.22
Step 4: report |E| = 1.22, so demand is elastic over this range.
Check: with the starting-value method you would get -20% / 20% = -1.00 and call it unit elastic. Same data, different classification. This is exactly why we fix one convention.

Slide 6 - Elasticity and total revenue
Total revenue TR = P x Q.
Before: $3.00 x 500 = $1,500 per day. After: $3.60 x 400 = $1,440 per day.
Rule: when demand is elastic, a price increase lowers total revenue; when demand is inelastic, a price increase raises total revenue; at unit elasticity total revenue does not change.
The coffee cart is consistent with the rule: elastic demand, price went up, revenue fell by $60 a day.

Slide 7 - What makes demand more elastic?
- Close substitutes are available (the dining hall sells drip coffee for $2.25)
- The good is a larger share of the budget
- A longer time horizon to adjust
- A narrowly defined market ("drip coffee at this cart" versus "caffeine")

Slide 8 - Exam notes
- Midterm 2 covers Weeks 5 to 8. Elasticity questions on Midterm 2 must use the midpoint formula; answers that use starting values get at most half credit.
- Show all four steps from Slide 5.
- The elasticity formula sheet is NOT provided on Midterm 2. Memorize the formulas.

Slide 9 - Preview of Week 7
Cross-price elasticity: the sign matters there (positive means substitutes, negative means complements), so we do NOT take absolute values for cross-price elasticity.

DLEC-CTX-G2.title: CS 261 Lecture 11 notes - Binary heaps and build-heap
DLEC-CTX-G2.text:
CS 261 - Data Structures
Lecture 11 Notes: Binary Heaps and Build-Heap
Prof. Tomasz Reinholt-Vega | Carrow Institute of Technology

1. What a binary heap is
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array that satisfies the heap-order property. In CS 261 we use MIN-heaps by default: every node's key is less than or equal to the keys of its children, so the smallest key sits at the root.

2. CS 261 array convention (differs from the 0-indexed code you will see online)
We store the heap 1-indexed. Index 0 is left empty (we write it as _).
- parent(i) = floor(i / 2)
- left(i) = 2i
- right(i) = 2i + 1
If you see parent(i) = floor((i - 1) / 2) and left(i) = 2i + 1 online, that is the 0-indexed layout. Both are correct for their own layout, but on CS 261 quizzes you must use the 1-indexed formulas.

3. Height convention
In CS 261 the height of a tree counts NODES on the longest root-to-leaf path, so a single node has height 1 and an empty tree has height 0. (Most textbooks count edges, so for them a single node has height 0.) With our convention a heap with n keys has height floor(log2 n) + 1. Example: n = 7 gives height 3.

4. Sift-down (heapify at index i)
Compare the key at i with its children. If the smaller child is smaller than the key at i, swap with that smaller child and repeat from the child's index. Stop when the key is no larger than both children or when i has no children. Cost: O(height).

5. Build-heap (bottom-up)
Call sift-down on i = floor(n / 2), floor(n / 2) - 1, ..., 1. Leaves (indices greater than floor(n / 2)) are already heaps, so we skip them.
Total cost is O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes live near the bottom and can only sift down a short distance; the sum of heights over all nodes is bounded by a linear function of n.

6. Worked example (show the array after every sift-down call; this is required on quizzes)
Input, n = 7: [_, 9, 4, 7, 1, 8, 2, 6]
Start at i = floor(7 / 2) = 3.
- sift-down(3): 7 vs children 2 (i=6) and 6 (i=7). Swap with 2. Array: [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(2): 4 vs children 1 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 1. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]
- sift-down(1): 9 vs children 1 (i=2) and 2 (i=3). Swap with 1. Continue at i=2: 9 vs children 4 (i=4) and 8 (i=5). Swap with 4. Index 4 has no children. Array: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]
Result: [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

7. Other operations
- peek-min: O(1), it is A[1].
- insert: put the key at A[n + 1], then sift-up. O(log n).
- extract-min: move A[n] to A[1], shrink the heap, sift-down(1). O(log n).
- Finding the MAXIMUM in a min-heap is not cheap: the max is somewhere among the leaves, so it takes O(n) in general.

8. Logistics
Quiz 4 (next Thursday) covers heaps: sift-down traces, build-heap traces, and the index formulas above. Traces must use the 1-indexed layout. Priority queues and heapsort are on Quiz 5, not Quiz 4.
Office hours this week move to Wednesday 3-5 pm in Lowry 118 because of the department colloquium.

DLEC-CTX-C1.title: ECON 214 TA recitation handout - Elasticity quick guide
DLEC-CTX-C1.text:
ECON 214 Recitation Handout - Week 6
Elasticity Quick Guide
Prepared by TA Marcus Delacroix-Byrne for the Friday recitation sections

Formula
Own-price elasticity of demand = % change in quantity demanded / % change in price, where each percentage change is computed from the ORIGINAL value:
% change in Q = (Q2 - Q1) / Q1
% change in P = (P2 - P1) / P1
Keep the negative sign. A demand elasticity of -1.5 should be written as -1.5 so the grader can see you know demand slopes down.

Classification
- E below -1 (for example -1.5): elastic
- E between -1 and 0: inelastic
- E equal to -1: for this course, treat unit elastic as elastic, since the revenue logic is the same.

Practice example: the Quad coffee cart
The cart raises the price of a small drip coffee from $3.00 to $3.60 and daily sales fall from 500 to 400 cups.
% change in Q = -100 / 500 = -20%
% change in P = 0.60 / 3.00 = 20%
E = -20% / 20% = -1.00, so demand here is elastic (unit elastic counts as elastic).

Total revenue
Revenue before: $1,500 per day. Revenue after: $1,440 per day. Because the cart is on the elastic side, revenue moves in the opposite direction from price.

Exam tips
- On Midterm 2 either the original-value method or the midpoint method gets full credit, so use whichever is faster for you.
- A formula sheet will be stapled to the back of Midterm 2, so you do not need to memorize the formulas.
- Cross-price elasticity: take the absolute value, same as own-price, and report it to two decimals.
- If a question does not say which price is the starting price, use the lower price as the base.

Office hours for recitation questions: Fridays 1-2 pm, Econ Commons table 4.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So remember, when demand is elastic and you raise the price, total revenue goes up, and that's exactly why the cart owner did it.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Okay, back to the coffee cart outside Benning Hall. Price goes from three dollars to three sixty.
PROFESSOR: Sales drop from five hundred cups a day to four hundred, and with our midpoint formula that's an elasticity of one point two two.
PROFESSOR: So demand is elastic over that range.
items.answer: The lecturer has the rule backwards. When demand is elastic, a price increase **lowers** total revenue, not raises it. Check the numbers: before, $3.00 times 500 cups is $1,500 a day. After, $3.60 times 400 cups is $1,440 a day. Revenue fell by $60, which is exactly what the elastic case predicts. The cart owner's price hike actually cost them money.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: explain gradient descent using an example from my own work experience so it actually sticks
items.answer: Gradient descent is just walking downhill on a loss surface: you compute the slope, then step opposite it. Picture tuning one setting in something I've built, changing it a little, and watching whether the result got better or worse. If it improved, keep going that direction; if not, reverse. The **learning rate** is step size, too big and you overshoot, too small and it crawls.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: accuracy vs precision?
conversation: PROFESSOR: One announcement, the career fair is Thursday in the student union, and the engineering firms are there from ten to two.
PROFESSOR: Bring printed copies of your resume, some recruiters still want paper.
items.answer: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value, while precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. You can have one without the other: a scale that always reads two pounds too heavy is precise but not accurate, and a scale that lands all over the place but averages out right is accurate but not precise. In practice you want both, and the gap between them usually tells you whether to fix a systematic bias or just tighten up your process.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: ok so what does it solve to, and show me how you get there
conversation: USER (typed to Natively): she wrote T(n) = 2T(n/2) + Theta(n) for merge sort and I have no idea how to read that

NATIVELY: That's a **recurrence relation**. It's a compact way of saying how much work merge sort does on an input of size n. Read it as: to sort n items, you do two sorts of half the items, plus some extra work that grows linearly with n.

The pieces: T(n) is the total time for n elements. The **2T(n/2)** means two subproblems, each half the size, because merge sort splits the array in two and recurses on both. The **Theta(n)** is the merge step, where you walk through both sorted halves and combine them, which takes time proportional to n.

So the whole line says: total time equals the time for the two halves plus the linear merge. Solving it gives Theta(n log n), which is the familiar merge sort running time.

NATIVELY: The **n/2** is the size of each half. Merge sort splits the array into two parts, and each part has half the elements, so a subproblem on n items becomes two subproblems on n/2 items each. That's why the term is 2T(n/2): two recursive calls, each on half the input.
items.answer:
To solve it, you keep expanding the recurrence until the subproblems hit size 1, then add up the work at each level.

Level 0: one problem of size n, work Theta(n).
Level 1: two problems of size n/2, total work 2 · Theta(n/2) = Theta(n).
Level 2: four problems of size n/4, total work 4 · Theta(n/4) = Theta(n).

The pattern: every level does Theta(n) total work, because doubling the number of subproblems exactly cancels halving their size. So the question becomes how many levels there are. You halve n until you reach 1, which takes log base 2 of n steps. That gives Theta(n) work per level times log n levels, so **Theta(n log n)**.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: So the Peace of Westphalia, 1648, ends the Thirty Years' War, and it's usually taught as the moment the modern system of sovereign states is born.
items.answer: The Peace of Westphalia is actually two treaties signed in 1648, at Münster and Osnabrück, and together they ended the Thirty Years' War and, in a separate settlement, the Eighty Years' War between Spain and the Dutch Republic. The reason it gets taught as the birth of the sovereign state system is that it shifted authority away from the papacy and the Holy Roman Emperor toward individual rulers, establishing the idea that each state has **territorial sovereignty** and that no outside power can dictate its internal affairs. It also introduced the notion of a **balance of power**, since the settlement was designed to prevent any single state from dominating Europe. So the "Westphalian system" is really a shorthand for that principle of non-interference in domestic affairs, even though historians debate how much of it was genuinely new in 1648 versus a gradual development.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: whats entropy
items.answer:
Entropy is a measure of how many ways a system can be arranged without changing how it looks from the outside. In thermodynamics it's often described as disorder, but the cleaner idea is missing information: the more arrangements that give the same observable state, the higher the entropy.

The classic formula is **S = k log W**, where S is entropy, k is Boltzmann's constant, and W is the number of microscopic arrangements matching the macrostate. In information theory Shannon entropy uses the same shape, **H = -Σ p log p**, measuring average surprise or uncertainty in a message.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: given my background, which parts of today's lecture on SQL joins can I safely skip?
items.answer:
I can't tell you what to skip based on your background, since I don't have it here. What I can do is tell you which parts of a joins lecture are usually safe to skim once you already know the basics.

If you're comfortable with inner joins and simple two-table queries, the parts worth skimming are the syntax refreshers and the basic Venn-diagram intuition. The parts worth staying awake for are the ones that trip people up in practice: how **NULL** values behave in joins, the difference between `ON` and `WHERE` in an outer join, and how a **left join** can quietly multiply rows when the right side has duplicates. Those are the ones that cause real bugs, not the ones that are easy to look up.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: And the printing press is the key here, Gutenberg's from around 1450, which is why Luther's Ninety-five Theses in 1517 spread across the German lands in a matter of weeks.
items.answer: Right, and the timing matters: movable type in Europe around 1450, and by 1517 Luther's theses were being printed and reprinted in German and Latin, so copies reached cities across the German lands within weeks rather than the months or years hand-copying would have taken. The press didn't create the ideas, it just made them impossible to contain.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: teach me Bayes' theorem properly. start from what conditional probability actually means, derive the formula, then walk me through a disease screening example with real numbers, and finish with the mistake people make most often with it.
items.answer:
Conditional probability is just probability after you learn something. P(A | B) means the chance of A, given that B is true, so you shrink the world down to only the cases where B happened and ask how often A sits inside that smaller world. Formally, P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B), as long as P(B) isn't zero.

Bayes' theorem falls straight out of that. Since P(A and B) equals P(B | A) times P(A), you can write the same joint probability two ways and solve for the one you want:

P(A | B) = P(B | A) · P(A) / P(B)

Here P(A) is the prior, what you believed before seeing B. P(B | A) is the likelihood, how well A predicts the evidence. P(A | B) is the posterior, your updated belief. And P(B) is the total probability of the evidence, which you usually expand as P(B | A)·P(A) + P(B | not A)·P(not A).

Now the screening example. Say a disease affects 1 in 1,000 people, so the prior P(D) is 0.001. The test catches 99% of sick people, so P(+ | D) is 0.99. It also falsely flags 5% of healthy people, so P(+ | not D) is 0.05. You test positive. What's the chance you actually have it?

The evidence term: P(+) = 0.99 × 0.001 + 0.05 × 0.999 = 0.00099 + 0.04995 = 0.05094. So P(D | +) = 0.00099 / 0.05094, which is about 0.019, or roughly 2%. A positive on a 99% accurate test still leaves you at about 2% because the disease is so rare that the false positives swamp the true ones.

The mistake people make most often is ignoring the base rate. They hear "99% accurate" and jump to 99% likely, forgetting that the prior P(D) does most of the work. The second most common slip is confusing P(+ | D) with P(D | +), which are very different numbers.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: explain simpler: what's the difference between a movement along the demand curve and a shift of the curve? she lost me
items.answer:
A movement along the curve happens when only the **price** changes. The curve stays put, you just slide to a different point on it.

A shift happens when something other than price changes, like income, tastes, or the price of a related good. Then the whole curve moves to a new position.

So the quick test: did price change? Slide along. Did anything else change? The curve shifts.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: teach me build-heap properly using his worked example: why we start at floor(n/2), what each sift-down does to the array, and why the whole thing is O(n) and not O(n log n).
items.answer:
Start at floor(n/2) because everything past it is a leaf, and a single node is already a valid heap. So the last node with children is floor(n/2), and we sift down from there back to the root.

In the example, n = 7, so we start at i = 3. Sift-down(3) swaps 7 with its smaller child 2, giving [_, 9, 4, 2, 1, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(2) swaps 4 with 1, giving [_, 9, 1, 2, 4, 8, 7, 6]. Sift-down(1) swaps 9 with 1, then 9 with 4, giving [_, 1, 4, 2, 9, 8, 7, 6]. Four swaps total.

It's O(n), not O(n log n), because most nodes sit near the bottom and can only fall a short distance. Summing each node's height gives a linear bound.

items.question: Okay. So if you want the derivative of sine x from first principles, you write sine of x plus h, expand it with the angle addition formula, and the whole thing comes down to two limits: sine h over h, and cosine h minus one over h.
conversation: PROFESSOR: Before we start, quick housekeeping. The problem set deadline moved to Monday at noon because of the fire drill.

items.answer:
That's right, and the two limits are where the work actually happens. The first one, sine h over h, goes to 1 as h goes to 0. The second, cosine h minus one over h, goes to 0. So the derivative collapses to cosine x.

If you want the full line: sine of x plus h is sine x cosine h plus cosine x sine h. Subtract sine x, group the terms, and you get sine x times (cosine h minus one) over h plus cosine x times sine h over h. Let h go to zero and you're left with cosine x.

items.question: using the slides' method, what's the elasticity if the cart cuts the price from 3.60 back to 3.00 and sales go from 400 back up to 500?
items.answer:
Using the midpoint formula, the price cut from $3.60 to $3.00 with sales rising from 400 to 500 gives the same magnitude as the slide example, just in the other direction.

Step 1: % change in Q = (500 - 400) / 450 = 0.2222, so 22.2%
Step 2: % change in P = (3.00 - 3.60) / 3.30 = -0.1818, so -18.2%
Step 3: E = 22.2% / -18.2% = -1.22
Step 4: report |E| = **1.22**, so demand is **elastic** over this range.

That's the point of the midpoint convention: reversing the direction gives the same 1.22, not the 1.00 you'd get from starting values.

items.question: So what happens if I increase the pressure on nitrogen plus three hydrogen going to two ammonia? Somebody?

NATIVELY: Le Chatelier's principle says a system at equilibrium responds to a disturbance by shifting in the direction that partially counteracts it. The classic cases: add more reactant and the reaction shifts toward products; increase pressure and it shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules; raise the temperature and it shifts in the endothermic direction, since that absorbs the added heat. It's a qualitative rule about which way the equilibrium moves, not how fast it gets there.
items.answer: Increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the side with fewer gas molecules. On the left you have four moles of gas, one nitrogen plus three hydrogen, and on the right just two moles of ammonia, so the system shifts toward ammonia. More ammonia at equilibrium, and that's exactly why the Haber process runs at high pressure.

items.answer:
Write **elastic**. The handout computes E = -20% / 20% = -1.00, and its own rule says that for this course unit elastic counts as elastic, since the revenue logic is the same. So the number is -1.00 and the label is elastic, which is exactly what she said in lecture.

items.role: USER: a student / learner. OTHER PARTY: the professor (lecture audio). Natively: private explanation for the student; need not be speakable.
items.question: she wrote upside-down A x, backwards E y, Loves(x, y) on the board, then wrote backwards E y, upside-down A x, Loves(x, y) and said they mean totally different things. what are those symbols, how do I read them out loud, and why does swapping the order change the meaning?
items.answer:
The upside-down A is the **universal quantifier**, read "for all." The backwards E is the **existential quantifier**, read "there exists."

So the first one, ∀x ∃y Loves(x, y), reads "for every x there exists a y such that x loves y." The second, ∃y ∀x Loves(x, y), reads "there exists a y such that for every x, x loves y."

The order matters because the quantifiers are nested, so each one's scope depends on which comes first. In the first, the y can be different for each x: everyone loves someone, possibly a different person each time. In the second, one single y works for everybody: there's one person whom everyone loves. Same symbols, same predicate, completely different claim.
